mainEntity.name: What is the throw keyword in Java?

acceptedAnswer.text: The throw keyword in Java is used to explicitly throw an exception from within a method or constructor. It transfers control flow from the current execution point to the nearest matching catch block in the call stack. Syntax: throw new ExceptionType(message); — the operand must be an instance of Throwable (or its subclass). When throw is executed, the current method stops immediately, and the JVM unwinds the call stack looking for a matching catch block. If none is found, the thread terminates with an unhandled exception message.

mainEntity.name: What is the difference between throw and throws in Java?

acceptedAnswer.text: throw is a statement inside a method/constructor body that actually throws an exception instance: throw new IOException('File not found'). throws is a keyword in the method signature that declares which checked exceptions the method might propagate to callers: void readFile() throws IOException. throw causes the exception to occur; throws warns callers that they must handle or propagate the declared exceptions. throw is used with a single exception instance; throws can list multiple exception types separated by commas. throw can throw both checked and unchecked exceptions; throws only needs to declare checked exceptions (RuntimeException subclasses need not be declared).

mainEntity.name: Can we throw a null in Java?

acceptedAnswer.text: Technically, 'throw null' compiles in Java, but at runtime it throws a NullPointerException — not the intended exception. This is because the throw statement evaluates its expression, finds null, and the JVM itself throws a NullPointerException as it attempts to process the null reference. The result is a confusing NPE instead of the intended exception. Never throw null — always create a proper exception instance: throw new IllegalArgumentException('reason'). If you must conditionally throw, use Objects.requireNonNull(exc, 'exception cannot be null') before throwing.

mainEntity.name: What is exception chaining in Java?

acceptedAnswer.text: Exception chaining (also called exception wrapping) is the practice of catching one exception and throwing a new exception that includes the original as its cause. Syntax: throw new NewException('message', originalException); The original exception is stored as the cause and is accessible via getCause(). Purpose: (1) Translate low-level exceptions (SQLException) into domain-level exceptions (RepositoryException) without losing the original diagnostic information. (2) Cross layer boundaries cleanly — service layer should not expose database-specific exceptions. The full chain is printed in stack traces, making debugging much easier than if the cause were lost.

mainEntity.name: Can we throw multiple exceptions from a single throw statement?

acceptedAnswer.text: No — a single throw statement can only throw one exception at a time. However, there are patterns to aggregate multiple exceptions: (1) Build a collection of errors, then throw one summary exception at the end (validation pattern). (2) Use a composite exception that holds a list of causes. (3) In parallel processing, use CompletableFuture which can capture multiple exceptions. The throws clause in a method signature CAN declare multiple exception types separated by commas — but that is about what might be thrown, not throwing multiple at once.

sections.title: What is the throw Keyword in Java?

blocks.text: The throw keyword in Java is used to explicitly throw an exception from any point inside a method, constructor, or block. It is the mechanism by which your code signals that something has gone wrong — an invalid argument, a violated business rule, a failed precondition, or an unexpected state — and that normal execution cannot continue.

When throw is executed, the current method stops immediately — no further statements in that method execute. The JVM begins unwinding the call stack, looking for the nearest catch block that can handle the thrown exception type. If a matching catch is found, execution transfers there. If no matching catch exists anywhere in the call stack, the thread terminates and the exception is printed to System.err.

The throw statement's operand must be an instance of java.lang.Throwable or any of its subclasses. In practice, you always throw either an Exception subclass (for recoverable conditions) or an Error subclass (for unrecoverable JVM-level conditions — almost never done by application code). The two main branches are checked exceptions (must be declared or caught) and unchecked exceptions (RuntimeException subclasses — no declaration required).

blocks.title: 🔑 throw at a Glance
blocks.text: Syntax: throw new ExceptionType("message"); — must be a Throwable instance. Effect: immediately stops current method, unwinds call stack, transfers to matching catch. throw vs throws: throw = the action of throwing; throws = method signature declaration of what might propagate. Throw checked exceptions: callers must handle or declare. Throw unchecked (RuntimeException): no forced handling by callers. Custom exceptions: extend Exception (checked) or RuntimeException (unchecked). Exception chaining: throw new NewException("msg", originalCause).

The throw statement has one simple form: the keyword throw followed by an expression that evaluates to a Throwable instance. Most commonly, this means throw new SomeException(message) — creating a new exception object and immediately throwing it. Code after a throw statement in the same block is unreachable and will cause a compile warning.

items.title: Basic Syntax
What Happens When throw Executes
items.text:
1. Current method stops at the throw statement.
2. JVM creates/uses the exception object with stack trace snapshot.
3. JVM unwinds call stack frame by frame.
4. Each frame's finally blocks execute during unwinding.
5. First matching catch block found → execution transfers there.
6. No matching catch found → thread terminates, stack trace printed.

blocks.text: Unchecked exceptions extend RuntimeException (or Error). They do not need to be declared in the throws clause or caught by callers — the compiler does not enforce handling. They represent programming errors or contract violations that could have been prevented by the calling code: null arguments, out-of-bounds indices, invalid states, arithmetic errors. Throwing an unchecked exception is how you enforce preconditions.

blocks.title: 💡 Standard Unchecked Exceptions — Choose the Right One
blocks.text: Java's standard library has well-defined unchecked exceptions for common programming errors. Use them precisely: NullPointerException — null reference where non-null expected (prefer Objects.requireNonNull()). IllegalArgumentException — caller passed a value that violates the method's contract. IllegalStateException — method called at wrong time / object in invalid state for the operation. IndexOutOfBoundsException — index out of valid range. ArithmeticException — arithmetic error (division by zero). UnsupportedOperationException — operation not implemented or intentionally unsupported. NumberFormatException — string cannot be parsed as a number. Using the correct standard exception makes your API immediately understandable to any Java developer.

Checked exceptions extend Exception (but not RuntimeException). The Java compiler enforces that any method throwing a checked exception must either declare it in its throws clause or catch and handle it internally. They represent recoverable conditions where the caller can reasonably be expected to handle the failure: file not found, network timeout, database connection lost.

blocks.label: ThrowChecked.java
lines: // ─── Declaring and throwing a checked exception ───────────────────────
// Method declares 'throws IOException' because it may throw it
public static String readFileContent(String filePath) throws IOException {
// ✅ throw checked exception — caller MUST handle or re-declare
throw new IOException("File not found: " + filePath);
throw new IOException("File is not readable: " + filePath);
public static void sendEmail(String to, String subject, String body)
// IllegalArgumentException is unchecked — but declared here for clarity
throw new IllegalArgumentException("Invalid email address: " + to);
throw new IllegalArgumentException("Email subject cannot be blank");
throw new IOException("SMTP server unreachable — check network");
// ─── Caller MUST handle or propagate checked exceptions ───────────────
// Bad input: Invalid email address: invalid-email

sections.title: throw in Constructors — Preventing Invalid Objects

blocks.text: Constructors are an ideal place to use throw — they enforce object invariants by preventing the creation of an object in an invalid state. If a constructor receives invalid arguments, it should throw an exception immediately rather than constructing a broken object that will fail later in an unpredictable location. This is the fail-fast principle: surface errors at the earliest possible moment.

blocks.label: ThrowInConstructor.java
lines: // ─── Guard clauses in constructor — throw on invalid state ─────────
throw new IllegalArgumentException("accountId must not be blank");
throw new IllegalArgumentException("holderName must not be blank");
"Initial deposit (₹%.2f) must be at least minimum balance (₹%.2f)",
// All validations passed — safe to assign fields
throw new IllegalArgumentException("Withdrawal amount must be positive");
"Withdrawal of ₹%.2f would breach minimum balance of ₹%.2f",
// Creation failed: Initial deposit (₹100.00) must be at

blocks.title: 💡 Fail-Fast in Constructors — The Golden Rule
blocks.text: A constructor that accepts invalid arguments and stores them is like a time bomb — the object will fail later, somewhere else, making the root cause hard to trace. Always validate in the constructor and throw immediately if invariants are violated. The stack trace will point directly to the construction site, making debugging trivial. Objects.requireNonNull(param, 'message') is the idiomatic null check — it throws NullPointerException with your message, making the check a one-liner. After all throw guards in a constructor, you can be confident that any code reaching the field assignments has passed all invariants.

While Java's standard exceptions cover many cases, custom exceptions are essential for expressing domain-specific failure conditions clearly. A custom exception class communicates what went wrong in business terms — InsufficientFundsException, ProductNotFoundException, OrderAlreadyShippedException — rather than generic technical terms. They also allow callers to catch specific failure types without catching everything.

blocks.label: CustomExceptions.java
lines: // ─── Custom CHECKED exception — caller must handle or declare ────────────
// Always provide at minimum: message constructor and cause constructor
public InsufficientFundsException(double requested, double available, Throwable cause) {
public double getShortfall()  { return requested - available; }
// ─── Custom UNCHECKED exception — no forced handling ─────────────────────
super("Product not found with id: " + productId);
super("Product not found with id: " + productId, cause);
public void processPayment(String productId, double amount, double walletBalance)
// Throws checked — MUST declare in throws clause
// Insufficient funds: requested ₹1500.00 but only ₹800.00 available

blocks.title: 📌 Custom Exception Design Rules
blocks.text: Every custom exception should follow these four rules: (1) Provide a message constructor: super(message). (2) Provide a cause constructor: super(message, cause) — for exception chaining. (3) Provide a combined constructor if useful: super(message, cause) with domain fields. (4) Add domain-specific context fields (productId, userId, errorCode) with getters — these let catch blocks extract structured information without parsing the message string. Prefer RuntimeException over Exception for domain exceptions in modern Spring/microservice architectures — checked exceptions create verbose propagation chains that add noise without benefit.

sections.title: throw vs throws — The Critical Distinction

blocks.text: These two keywords look similar but serve entirely different purposes. throw is a statement that causes an exception to occur. throws is a method signature keyword that declares what checked exceptions a method might propagate. Confusing them is one of the most common Java beginner mistakes.

rows: Actually throws (causes) an exception at runtime
Declares which checked exceptions may propagate to callers
Inside method body, constructor, or block
After parameter list, before method body: void m() throws X
One at a time — throw new X()
Only checked exceptions need declaration (RuntimeException doesn't)
Mandatory for checked exceptions not caught inside the method
Callers must catch or re-declare listed checked exceptions

blocks.label: ThrowVsThrows.java
lines: // 'throws' in signature — declares what MIGHT propagate
throw new IllegalArgumentException("Input is null"); // ← throw (action)
// IllegalArgumentException is unchecked — no throws declaration needed
throw new IOException("Empty input cannot be processed"); // ← throw
// IOException IS checked — MUST appear in throws clause above
throw new ParseException("Expected format: YYYY-MM-DD", 0); // ← throw
// Method that CATCHES internally — no throws needed
// No throws needed here — all checked exceptions caught above
// Method that PROPAGATES — must re-declare throws
parseAndProcess(content); // delegates — its checked exs propagate

sections.title: Exception Chaining — Wrapping the Root Cause

blocks.text: Exception chaining (also called exception wrapping or cause chaining) is the practice of catching a low-level exception and rethrowing it wrapped in a higher-level exception — preserving the original as the cause. This is critical for cross-layer exception translation: the service layer should not expose SQLException to the controller — it should throw a domain-specific RepositoryException while keeping the original SQLException accessible for debugging.

blocks.label: ExceptionChaining.java
lines: // Custom exception hierarchy for a payment service
super(message, cause); // ← stores original exception as cause
static void savePaymentToDb(double amount) throws java.sql.SQLException {
throw new java.sql.SQLException("Connection reset: host unreachable");
// ✅ Wrap with context — preserve root cause
"Failed to persist payment of ₹" + amount, e); // 'e' is the cause
static void processPayment(String orderId, double amount) {
// ✅ Wrap again with higher-level business context
"Payment processing failed for order: " + orderId, e);
// ✅ Full chain printed automatically by printStackTrace()
// e.printStackTrace(); // prints all three with 'Caused by:' markers
// PaymentException  : Payment processing failed for order: ORD-4521
// DatabaseException : Failed to persist payment of ₹2500.0
// Root SQLException : Connection reset: host unreachable

blocks.title: ⚠️ Never Lose the Cause — The Worst Exception Anti-Pattern
blocks.text: The most damaging exception mistake: catch (SQLException e) { throw new DatabaseException('DB error'); } — the original SQLException with its error code, SQL state, and stack trace is completely lost. The 'Caused by:' chain in the stack trace is how you diagnose production issues. Always pass the caught exception as the cause: throw new DatabaseException('DB error', e). This single habit prevents hours of debugging time. If you see exception constructors in your codebase that don't take a 'cause' parameter, add them immediately — they are incomplete.

Rethrowing means catching an exception and then throwing it again — either the same instance or a new wrapped exception. The main use cases are: adding logging or context before propagating, doing partial cleanup in a catch block, and conditional handling (handle some cases, rethrow others). Java 7+ allows rethrowing with precise type inference, and Java 7's multi-catch reduces boilerplate.

blocks.label: Rethrowing.java
lines: // ─── Pattern 1: Log then rethrow same exception ──────────────────────
public static void loadConfig(String path) throws IOException {
if (!new File(path).exists()) throw new IOException("Not found: " + path);
throw e; // ← rethrow SAME instance — stack trace preserved
// Handle format error — translate to more meaningful exception
"Port must be a number, got: '" + value + "'", e);
// NumberFormatException is the cause — not lost
public static void executeTransaction() throws Exception {
public static void processInput(String input) throws Exception {
if (input == null) throw new NullPointerException("null input");
// ✅ Multi-catch — handle both the same way
throw e; // rethrow — type is preserved accurately
// ─── Pattern 5: Wrap into RuntimeException for unchecked propagation ─
// Wrap checked in unchecked — no throws declaration needed
throw new RuntimeException("Failed to read: " + path, e);
// Port must be a number, got: 'abc'

blocks.text: Throwing inside a catch block is one of the most powerful and commonly used patterns in Java exception handling. It enables: adding log context before propagation, translating low-level exceptions to domain exceptions, doing partial recovery followed by re-escalation, and conditional handling based on the exception's state.

sections.title: Guard Clauses with throw — Fail-Fast Precondition Checking

blocks.text: The guard clause pattern uses throw statements at the beginning of a method to reject invalid inputs early — before any real work begins. Each guard is a concise if-throw statement that validates one precondition. Guard clauses flatten deeply nested validation logic, make preconditions explicit and self-documenting, and ensure the method body only executes with valid, contract-compliant input.

blocks.label: GuardClauses.java
lines: // ─── Guard clauses — validate all preconditions upfront ───────────────
throw new IllegalArgumentException("customerId must not be blank");
throw new IllegalArgumentException("deliveryAddress must not be blank");
throw new IllegalArgumentException("Order must contain at least one item");
"Order cannot have more than " + MAX_ITEMS + " items, got: " + items.size());
throw new IllegalArgumentException("Order total must be positive: " + total);
// At this point: customerId, items, address, token are all valid
// total is positive and within limits
record OrderItem(String name, double price, int quantity) {}
// Rejected: Order must contain at least one item

blocks.text: throw null is a syntactically valid Java statement — it compiles without error. But at runtime, the JVM attempts to process the null reference as a Throwable, which itself causes a NullPointerException to be thrown. The resulting NPE has a confusing, misleading stack trace — it looks like a normal NPE from your code, not like the intended exception. This trap is most commonly encountered through a null reference variable.

blocks.label: ThrowNull.java
lines: // ─── Direct throw null — compiles but throws NPE at runtime ────────
throw null; // ← compiles! but at runtime → NullPointerException
System.out.println("Caught NPE from throw null: " + e.getClass().getName());
// Not the intended exception — confusing stack trace
// ─── More common trap: null reference variable ────────────────────
RuntimeException exception = null; // forgot to initialize!
// Developer expects to throw 'exception' but it's null
// throw exception; // ← throws NPE, NOT a meaningful exception!
throw safeException; // ✅ safe — will only throw if non-null
String errorMessage = getError(); // might return null
//    If errorMessage is null, exception is created with null message
//    Not the same as throw null — but a null message is confusing

blocks.title: ⚠️ Three Rules to Avoid the throw null Trap
blocks.text: Rule 1: Never write 'throw null' explicitly — always throw a new exception instance or a pre-created, non-null variable. Rule 2: If you store an exception in a variable before throwing, always initialize it to a default: RuntimeException ex = new RuntimeException('default'). Rule 3: If the exception instance comes from external code or a method return, null-check it before throwing. The NullPointerException thrown by 'throw null' appears to originate from the throw statement itself — making the stack trace look like a legitimate NPE from your code, not a logic error. Static analysis tools (SonarQube, IntelliJ inspections) can detect throw null patterns — enable these checks.
These mistakes with throw are consistently found in Java code and often produce confusing errors, lost information, or incorrect exception behavior.

if (input == null) throw new Exception("null"); // too broad!
// ✅ Fix: throw new IllegalArgumentException("input must not be null");
// ❌ MISTAKE 2: Losing the cause — throw new X(e.getMessage()) only
// ❌ MISTAKE 3: Catching and rethrowing as new instance (loses stack trace)
public static void loseStackTrace() throws Exception {
throw new Exception(e.getMessage()); // ❌ new instance = new stack trace
// Original stack trace from where exception occurred is GONE
// ❌ MISTAKE 4: throw in finally block — suppresses original exception
public static void throwInFinally() throws Exception {
throw new RuntimeException("finally error"); // ❌ HIDES original!
// 'original error' is now swallowed — finally exception wins
// ✅ Fix: avoid throw in finally; use try-with-resources instead
// ❌ MISTAKE 5: Throwing too early before all validation

blocks.text: These throw-related anti-patterns appear in code reviews and lead to unmaintainable error handling, lost diagnostic information, and confusing caller APIs.

items.title: throw new Exception() — The Generic Exception Smell
items.text: Throwing the base Exception class provides no information about what kind of failure occurred. Callers cannot selectively catch it — they must catch Exception (which also catches all checked exceptions) or ignore it. Always throw the most specific exception type that accurately describes the failure: IllegalArgumentException for bad input, IllegalStateException for wrong state, IOException for I/O failures, your own custom domain exceptions for business rule violations. 'throw new Exception(message)' in application code is a code smell that signals unfinished error handling design.

items.title: Using Exceptions for Normal Control Flow
items.text: Writing code that uses exceptions to handle expected, non-exceptional conditions is a serious performance and readability problem. Example: try { return map.get(key); } catch (NullPointerException e) { return default; } — use map.getOrDefault() instead. Or using NumberFormatException as a way to detect non-numeric strings in a validation loop. Exceptions have non-trivial overhead (stack trace capture). Use if-else, Optional, return values, or validation methods for expected conditions — reserve exceptions for truly exceptional failures.

items.title: Throwing from finally Block
items.text: A throw statement inside a finally block silently swallows any exception that was in flight from the try or catch block. If try threw IOException and finally throws RuntimeException, the IOException is permanently lost — callers only see RuntimeException. This is especially insidious because the code looks correct. Fix: avoid throw in finally. If cleanup code can fail, catch its exception internally. Java's try-with-resources handles this correctly — suppressed exceptions are recorded on the primary exception via addSuppressed().

items.title: Throwing Error Subclasses from Application Code
items.text: Error and its subclasses (OutOfMemoryError, StackOverflowError, AssertionError) represent JVM-level unrecoverable conditions — they should almost never be thrown by application code. Catching and rethrowing Error is even worse — it prevents the JVM from performing necessary cleanup. Application code should throw Exception subclasses. The only legitimate case for application code to throw Error is for truly unrecoverable situations where the JVM itself should terminate — extremely rare and almost always better handled by letting a RuntimeException propagate.

items.title: Reporting Multiple Errors One-at-a-Time
items.text: In validation scenarios, throwing on the first error forces the caller to fix one issue, resubmit, get another error, fix it, resubmit — a frustrating loop. Better pattern: collect ALL validation errors into a list, then throw a single ValidationException containing all errors at once. Users get 'name is blank; email is invalid; age is out of range' in one response rather than three sequential responses. This requires designing a validation exception that holds a List<String> of error messages.

items.title: Missing Error Messages or Poor Message Quality
items.text: throw new IllegalArgumentException() — empty message — is useless in a stack trace. throw new RuntimeException('error') — generic message — barely better. Good exception messages should answer three questions: WHAT was wrong (the field or operation), WHAT the actual value was (include it), and WHAT was expected. Example: throw new IllegalArgumentException('age must be between 0 and 150, got: ' + age) vs throw new IllegalArgumentException('invalid age'). The first is immediately actionable; the second requires debugging to understand.

blocks.text: The following examples demonstrate professional throw usage patterns from real enterprise Java codebases — a validation service with aggregate errors and a repository layer with exception translation.

super("Validation failed with " + errors.size() + " error(s): " + errors);
// ─── Aggregate validation — collect ALL errors, throw once ───────────

errors.add("username: must be between 3 and 30 characters, got: "
errors.add("username: may only contain letters, digits, and underscores");
errors.add("email: invalid format — must contain '@' and '.'");
errors.add("password: must be at least 8 characters");
errors.add("password: must contain at least one uppercase letter");
errors.add("password: must contain at least one digit");
errors.add("age: must be at least 13, got: " + age);
// ─── Throw ONCE with ALL errors collected ────────────────────────
//   - email: invalid format — must contain '@' and '.'
//   - password: must be at least 8 characters
//   - age: must be at least 13, got: 10

sections.title: Java throw Interview Questions — Beginner to Advanced

blocks.text: These questions are consistently asked in Java mid-level and senior interviews, OCPJP certification exams, and design-focused technical rounds covering exception handling.

items.q: Q1. What is the throw keyword in Java? How does it work?
items.a: The throw keyword explicitly throws an exception from within a method, constructor, or block. Syntax: throw new ExceptionType('message'). When throw executes: (1) The current method stops immediately — no further statements run. (2) The JVM captures a stack trace at the throw point. (3) Any finally blocks in the call chain execute during stack unwinding. (4) The JVM walks up the call stack looking for a matching catch block. (5) If found, execution transfers to the catch block. (6) If not found at the top of the stack, the thread terminates and the exception is printed to System.err. The operand must be a Throwable instance — throw null compiles but causes NullPointerException at runtime.

items.q: Q2. What is the difference between throw and throws in Java?
items.a: throw is a statement inside a method body that actually throws (causes) an exception: throw new IOException('failed'). throws is a keyword in the method signature that declares which checked exceptions the method may propagate: void read() throws IOException. throw occurs at runtime; throws is a compile-time declaration. throw uses a single exception instance; throws lists types separated by commas. throw can throw both checked and unchecked; throws declaration is only required for checked exceptions (RuntimeException subclasses need not be declared). A method can use throw without throws if it only throws unchecked exceptions. A method can have throws without any throw if it delegates to other methods that may throw.

items.q: Q3. Can we throw a checked exception without declaring it in throws?
items.a: No — attempting to throw a checked exception (any Exception subclass that is not a RuntimeException) without declaring it in the throws clause causes a compile-time error: 'unreported exception X; must be caught or declared to be thrown'. The only exception (no pun intended): if the checked exception is caught within the same method before it can propagate, no throws declaration is needed. Unchecked exceptions (RuntimeException and its subclasses) can always be thrown without any throws declaration. This is the fundamental difference between checked and unchecked exceptions.

items.q: Q4. What is exception chaining and how is it implemented with throw?
items.a: Exception chaining (wrapping) preserves the original exception when translating it to a higher-level exception. Implementation: catch (LowLevelException original) { throw new HighLevelException('message', original); }. The second constructor argument stores original as the cause. Access the cause via: getCause(). Purpose: (1) Translate technical exceptions (SQLException) to domain exceptions (RepositoryException) across layers. (2) Never lose diagnostic information — the full chain appears in stack traces as 'Caused by:' entries. The critical rule: ALWAYS pass the caught exception as the cause when wrapping — throw new HighLevelException(e.getMessage()) WITHOUT passing e loses the original stack trace and error code permanently.

items.q: Q5. What is the effect of a throw statement inside a finally block?
items.a: A throw inside a finally block is extremely dangerous — it silently suppresses any exception that was already in flight from the try or catch block. Example: try { throw new IOException('original'); } finally { throw new RuntimeException('finally'); } — the IOException is completely lost. The caller only sees RuntimeException('finally') with no indication that IOException ever occurred. Java's try-with-resources (AutoCloseable) handles this correctly: if both the try body and close() throw, close()'s exception is added as a 'suppressed' exception via addSuppressed(), preserving both. Fix: avoid throw in finally; handle cleanup exceptions internally.

items.q: Q6. Should you create custom checked exceptions or unchecked exceptions?
items.a: Modern Java practice (especially Spring, microservices, Java 8+): prefer unchecked (RuntimeException subclasses) for domain exceptions. Reasons: (1) Checked exceptions create noisy throws declarations that propagate through all layers. (2) Checked exceptions tempt developers to catch-and-ignore to 'make the compiler happy'. (3) They violate Open/Closed Principle — adding a new exception type forces signature changes throughout the call chain. Use checked exceptions when: the caller CAN realistically handle the failure and SHOULD be forced to deal with it (IOException for file operations, SQLException in JDBC code). Use unchecked for: domain violations, precondition failures, and most application-level errors where callers will either handle them globally or let them propagate to an error handler.

items.q: Q7. What happens when you execute 'throw null' in Java?
items.a: 'throw null' compiles without error because the compiler only verifies the throw operand is a Throwable reference — null satisfies that. At runtime, the JVM attempts to process the null reference as a Throwable, which triggers a NullPointerException thrown by the JVM itself. The resulting NPE has a misleading stack trace — it points to the throw statement, not to the actual logic error. The most dangerous version: RuntimeException ex = null; ... throw ex; — if ex is never initialized, same result. Prevention: always throw new ExceptionType() or a verified non-null variable. Never store exceptions in variables you might forget to initialize.

items.q: Q8. What is the best message format for exception messages?
items.a: Good exception messages follow the pattern: WHAT-went-wrong + ACTUAL-value + EXPECTED-value/constraint. Examples: 'Age must be between 0 and 150, got: -5' (what: age constraint, actual: -5, expected: 0-150). 'Amount must be positive, got: -1000.0 for order ORD-421' (what + context). 'Cannot withdraw ₹5000: balance ₹2000 below minimum ₹500' (state + values). Bad examples: 'Invalid input' (no specifics), 'Error' (useless), '' (empty). Including the actual invalid value is the most critical part — it makes the error immediately reproducible without attaching a debugger. Exception messages are read by developers during debugging — treat them as developer documentation.

items.q: Q9. What are guard clauses and how do they use throw?
items.a: Guard clauses are if-throw statements at the beginning of a method that reject invalid input before any actual work begins. Pattern: if (param == null) throw new IllegalArgumentException('param must not be null'); Each guard is a one-liner that validates one precondition. Benefits: (1) Fail-fast — errors detected at the earliest point, stack trace points to the construction/call site. (2) Flat code — the method body (happy path) runs without nested if-else. (3) Self-documenting — preconditions are explicit and visible at the top of the method. (4) No invalid objects — constructors with guards prevent broken object creation. Contrast with deeply nested if-else validation which buries the happy path in indentation and makes it hard to see what state is valid.

items.q: Q10. How do you design a validation system that reports all errors at once instead of one-at-a-time?
items.a: Pattern: collect all validation errors into a List<String>, then throw one exception containing the full list. (1) Create a custom ValidationException: class ValidationException extends RuntimeException { private final List<String> errors; ... }. (2) Validate each field, adding to the list (no throwing): if (email.isBlank()) errors.add('email: must not be blank'). (3) After all validation: if (!errors.isEmpty()) throw new ValidationException(errors). (4) Callers catch ValidationException and display all errors at once. Benefits: users see all problems in one response instead of playing fix-one-error-at-a-time. Used by: Spring Validation (@Valid + BindingResult), Hibernate Validator (ConstraintViolationException holds a set of violations), API frameworks (400 Bad Request with a body listing all issues).

sections.title: Conclusion — throw: The Language of Failure in Java

blocks.text: The throw keyword is how Java programs communicate failure. Mastering it means understanding not just the syntax, but the discipline of exception design: when to throw, what to throw, how to preserve information through chains, and how to make exceptions self-documenting through meaningful messages and structured context fields.

The hallmarks of professional throw usage: guard clauses at the top of every method with specific, value-inclusive messages; custom domain exceptions with cause constructors; exception chaining that never loses the root cause; aggregate validation that reports all errors at once; and no throw in finally blocks. These habits alone will put your exception handling in the top tier of Java code quality.

items.q: What is the throw keyword in Java?
items.a: The throw keyword explicitly throws an exception from within a method, constructor, or block. Syntax: throw new ExceptionType('message'). When executed, the current method stops immediately, the JVM unwinds the call stack executing finally blocks along the way, and transfers control to the nearest matching catch block. If no catch is found, the thread terminates. The operand must be a Throwable instance.

items.q: What is the difference between throw and throws in Java?
items.a: throw is a statement inside a method body that actually causes an exception: throw new IOException('failed'). throws is a keyword in the method signature that declares which checked exceptions may propagate: void read() throws IOException. throw is runtime action; throws is compile-time declaration. throw uses one exception instance; throws lists multiple types. throws declaration is required only for checked exceptions — unchecked RuntimeExceptions need no declaration.

items.q: Can we throw a null in Java?
items.a: throw null compiles but causes NullPointerException at runtime — the JVM throws NPE when it tries to process the null reference. Never throw null. Always throw a new exception instance or a verified non-null variable. The NPE from throw null has a misleading stack trace that looks like a regular null dereference, making it hard to diagnose.

items.q: What is exception chaining in Java?
items.a: Exception chaining preserves the original exception when wrapping it in a higher-level exception: throw new HighLevelException('message', originalException). The original is stored as the cause, accessible via getCause(). Purpose: translate technical exceptions across layers without losing root cause diagnostic information. Always pass the caught exception as the cause — throw new X(e.getMessage()) without 'e' loses the original stack trace permanently.

items.q: Can we throw multiple exceptions from a single throw statement?
items.a: No — one throw statement throws one exception. For multiple errors, collect them in a List<String> and throw one exception containing all errors: if (!errors.isEmpty()) throw new ValidationException(errors). This is the aggregate validation pattern — users see all problems in one response. The throws clause in a method signature CAN declare multiple types (throws A, B, C) but that is about what MIGHT be thrown, not throwing multiple at once.
